abstract: The Anthropic Economic Index report introduces five new economic primitives to measure AI's impact on the labor market by analyzing 1 million Claude.ai conversations and 1 million API transcripts from November 2025. The analysis reveals that computer/mathematical tasks account for ~33% of Claude.ai conversations and ~50% of API traffic, with concentrated usage among coding-related tasks; however, regional adoption is rapidly converging in the US (projected 2-5 year equalization across states) while remaining geographically uneven globally. The findings indicate that Claude succeeds on most tasks but with declining success on more complex ones, and that task automation would produce net deskilling across most occupations since AI handles higher-education tasks that are often the most skilled components of jobs.
keyFindings: Computer and mathematical tasks represent 33% of Claude.ai conversations and 46-50% of API traffic, though this share has declined from a peak of 40% in March 2025 to 34% in November 2025 on Claude.ai.

Within the US, the Anthropic AI Usage Index shows rapid convergence, with estimates suggesting usage parity across states could be reached in 2-5 years—approximately 10x faster than historical diffusion rates for economically consequential technologies.

Claude succeeds at most tasks overall, but success rates decline substantially as task complexity increases, with more complex tasks (requiring greater human education) showing lower success rates across countries.

Geographic variation in Claude usage is strongly predicted by GDP per capita globally (1% increase in GDP per capita associated with 0.7% increase in usage) and by workforce composition within the US (each 1% increase in computer/mathematical workers associated with 0.36% higher usage per capita).

When factoring in success rates, adjusted productivity estimates from task automation decline from 1.8 to approximately 1.0 percentage points of annual labor productivity growth, reflecting current model reliability limitations.
methodology: Analysis of 1 million randomly sampled Claude.ai conversations (Free, Pro, and Max) and 1 million first-party (1P) API transcripts from November 13-20, 2025. The study employs privacy-preserving analysis using Claude as a classifier to assign conversations to five economic primitives (task complexity, human/AI skills, use case, AI autonomy, task success). Validation of classifiers conducted against human ratings on small transcript samples for Claude.ai and internal/synthetic data for API data. Geographic analysis uses IP geolocation (ISO-3166 codes); US state analysis stratified by workforce composition. Diffusion estimates derived through ordinary least squares (OLS), weighted least squares (WLS), and two-stage least squares (2SLS) regression modeling proportional convergence toward steady state.
qualifiers: Estimates based on only three months of data (August-November 2025), creating substantial uncertainty in diffusion projections. Classifiers are directionally accurate but not exact, with authors noting they 'may deviate somewhat from human ratings.' US state-level analysis limited by smaller sample sizes and may not achieve statistical significance for some relationships. Privacy filtering excludes cells with fewer than 15 conversations and 5 unique user accounts globally. API data limited to single input-output pairs rather than full conversation trajectories, limiting analysis of multi-turn interactions. Sampling noise and attenuation bias acknowledged as concerns in diffusion estimates. Productivity growth estimates reflect current model capabilities and may change with future improvements. Preliminary findings note that 'diffusion may ultimately proceed more slowly in the months and years to come.'
